This is a big topic, so I have to focus narrowly to be coherent.

Scientists who study human intelligence have been doing so for a long time. A common theme has existed for centuries. No matter what intellectual ability was measured, it seemed to be linked in some way to IQ scores, which crudely is today referred to as 'g' by the scientists.

It is very common, actually it is banal, for students and laypeople to dismiss IQ scores as nonsense. Most of them don't realize that IQ scores are extremely easy to replicate scientifically and that of all the scientific research on intelligence, IQ is by far the most replicated, which is the same thing as saying it is the most scientific metric.

To use an analogy, human brains perform operations (I won't call it computation, but it's close enough to use similar metaphors).

Now some people have great eyesight which helps them perceive more adeptly. Some people have excellent memories. Some people are highly creative. What scientists found is that all these traits are linked.

Some people perform operations at a slower rate than others. While some people may excel in some areas and not others, there is a general trend, which is that if your IQ is high, it's also likely that you are healthy, have good eyesight, have an excellent memory and so on.

This makes sense because we're talking about a complex system. Mutations are usually bad. High IQ people with birth defects etc, they exist, but they're much rarer than the healthy high IQ people. A high IQ person is somebody who is optimized genetically. Which not only means intelligence, but also attractiveness, health and other positive qualities.

This brings me to comparative advantage. It's an economic term. It means we should trade with each other. Here is an example. Suppose it is easier to grow oranges in Mexico than in Canada. Suppose it is easier to rear sheep for wool in Canada. The trade should be orange juice for wool, and each nation is more wealthy for that.

Suppose there existed a perfect country. It would be equally capable of wool and orange juice production. It has a flawed neighbour, which can produce some quantity of oranges. It now makes sense for the perfect country to focus on wool production despite being capable of orange farming. This is because if it split its efforts it would wind up less wealthy than if it cooperated with the poorer nation and traded for less efficiently farmed oranges.

Something similar is true in genetics. Different racial groups (and subgroups, and classes) have different intellectual dispositions. The stereotypes are true. Blacks are unusually gifted at music, Asians are unusually good at mathematics and Jews are unusually well suited to studying theoretical physics.

These are broad generalizations of course. But when you examine the world you see clearly that different racial groups have monopolized certain areas of production. 1488 will obsess over the Jews but it's true of every race, they all have a distinct tendency to fit into specific economic niches, often to extreme levels.

Now to Lewontin's fallacy. It is is very popular and wrong. Lewontin measured the genetic differences between groups of humans, found that the % difference was tiny, and declared that 'race' held "virtually no genetic or taxonomic significance".

From the Wiki on the subject: Most of the information that distinguishes populations is hidden in the correlation structure of the data.
